Guru Tegh Bahadur

Stories of the Sikh Gurus

Guru Tegh Bahadur

The Shield of India

In everyday English — the whole story of the ninth Guru

Stories by Eku

How to Read · · BEFORE WE BEGIN

Read it out loud. This story was made to be told. Read slowly, as if you were sitting among family at home — with the morning of Amritsar and the silence of Bakala in the background.

The yellow boxes are the characters speaking in their own words. Change your voice a little when you read them — Tegh Bahadur's calm and grave, Makhan Shah's amazed, and nine-year-old Gobind's clear and fearless.

(The purple cues) tell you where to pause, whisper, or raise your voice. They are for the reader, not the listener.

At the end of every part, the green box — Pause and think. Stop there. Ask questions. Let the listener speak. In this story, those questions matter as much as the story.

There are two kinds of things in this book — Tegh Bahadur's own bani, written in the Guru Granth Sahib, and the stories of the tradition, told in the sangat for centuries. Where a story comes from the tradition, the book says so plainly — 'the tradition tells us'. Where the words are Tegh Bahadur's own, the book names them.

This book's main story comes from Tegh Bahadur's bani and the traditional life stories. The full list of sources is at the end of the book.

Who's Who · · WHO'S WHO

Guru Tegh Bahadur — the heart of this story. Born in Amritsar, the youngest son of Guru Hargobind, first called Tyag Mal, then Tegh Bahadur. Twenty-six years of meditation at Bakala, and the ninth Guru in 1664. The Shield of India.

Guru Hargobind — the sixth Guru of the Sikhs, Tegh Bahadur's father. He was the first Guru to take up both swords — miri and piri, the worldly and the spiritual.

Mata Nanaki — Tegh Bahadur's mother. Bakala was her village.

Mata Gujri — Tegh Bahadur's wife. Their son Gobind Rai later became the tenth Guru.

Guru Har Rai and Guru Har Krishan — the seventh and eighth Gurus. Har Krishan's dying words — 'Baba Bakale' — are what led Tegh Bahadur to the guruship.

Dhirmal — the grandson of Guru Hargobind, the son of Baba Gurditta. He too claimed the guruship.

Makhan Shah Lubana — a wealthy trader, whose search placed Tegh Bahadur on the guruship.

Pandit Kirpa Ram — the leader of the Kashmiri Pandits, who came to Anandpur in 1675.

Bhai Mati Das, Bhai Sati Das and Bhai Dyal Singh — the Guru's three companions, who went with him to Delhi and were martyred with him.

Bhai Jaita — a disciple of the Guru, who carried the Guru's head to Anandpur in the dark of night.

Lakhi Shah Vanjara — a disciple of the Guru, near whose house the Guru's body was cremated.

Aurangzeb — the emperor of India, on whose orders the Guru was martyred in Delhi.

Gobind Rai — Tegh Bahadur's son. He was nine years old at the time of the martyrdom — and he became the next Guru.

1 · Birth — Amritsar · · BIRTH — AMRITSAR

Amritsar — the holiest city of the Sikhs, where the sarovar of the Harmandir Sahib shone. There, in 1621, on the morning of 1 April 1621, a child was born. He was the youngest son of Guru Hargobind — and his name was Tyag Mal.

Tyag Mal had four elder brothers — Baba Gurditta, Suraj Mal, Ani Rai and Atal Rai — and an elder sister, Bibi Viro. The house held swords and horses, and bani too — because Hargobind had given the Sikhs both things — miri and piri — the sword that protects the world, and the sword of the Name of God.

Tyag Mal was different from childhood. He learned to wield the sword and to ride, but his heart did not stay long in noise. He would sit quietly and think — as if a deep river flowed inside him, whose sound only he could hear.

Tyag Mal was married at a young age to Gujri — who later became known as Mata Gujri. A home was made, a family grew. But the silence in Tyag Mal's heart stayed — he spoke little, and listened much.

The date of birth — 1 April 1621

Tegh Bahadur was born on 1 April 1621 in Amritsar — this date is recorded in the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism and by modern scholars. His first name was Tyag Mal, and he was the youngest son of Guru Hargobind.

The year of the marriage — 1632 or 1633?

Tyag Mal's marriage to Mata Gujri took place on 3 February 1632 — though some sources give the same date as 1633. This book follows 1632 in the main story, which is the year most sources record.

Pause and think — Tyag Mal spoke little and listened much. Do you think a person who stays quiet is weak — or is there a strength in silence too?

2 · From Tyag Mal to Tegh Bahadur · · FROM TYAG MAL TO TEGH BAHADUR

When Tyag Mal grew up, the times were not peaceful. The Sikhs were clashing with the Mughal emperors, and Guru Hargobind had often had to take up the sword. Tyag Mal too went with his father into battle — and in one battle — the Battle of Kartarpur — he showed such bravery that everyone kept watching him.

The tradition tells us that after the battle, Guru Hargobind looked at his son and said — from today your name is Tegh Bahadur — the brave swordsman, the brave bearer of the sword. The boy who was Tyag Mal — the renouncer — was now called Tegh Bahadur.

This name was not only about the sword. 'Tyag' means — to give up, to renounce — and 'tegh' means — the sword. In Tegh Bahadur's life these two things walked together — he took up the sword, and he gave up everything too. That was the secret of his name.

In 1644, Guru Hargobind passed away. The guruship went to his grandson Har Rai — Tegh Bahadur's nephew. Tegh Bahadur did not ask for the guruship. He went with his mother Nanaki and his wife Gujri to Bakala — Nanaki's village, near Amritsar.

The Battle of Kartarpur — how he got his name

Tegh Bahadur was given his name by Guru Hargobind after the bravery he showed in the Battle of Kartarpur — this is recorded in the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism. The year of the battle appears as both 1634 and 1635 in the old writings, so this book gives no year for the battle in the main story.

Who got the guruship — Har Rai

After Hargobind, the guruship went to his grandson Har Rai — Tegh Bahadur was not a claimant at that time. This matters to remember, because later the guruship returned to Bakala — to Tegh Bahadur.

Pause and think — Tegh Bahadur did not ask for the guruship — he went quietly to Bakala. Do you think there is a way to receive something without asking for it?

3 · Twenty-Six Years of Silence at Bakala · · TWENTY-SIX YEARS OF SILENCE AT BAKALA

Bakala was a small village — wells, baolis, fields, and quiet. Tegh Bahadur lived there in a simple house — with his mother Nanaki and his wife Gujri. He did the work of the house, he looked after the family — but most of his time went to one thing — meditation.

The tradition tells us that Tegh Bahadur had a bhora made at Bakala — a small cell under the ground — where he sat for hours in meditation. He repeated the Name, he sang bani, and he stayed silent. Outside, the world was changing — the guruship had passed from Har Rai to Har Krishan — but in Bakala, time seemed to have stopped.

This silence lasted twenty-six years — from 1644 to 1664. For twenty-six years Tegh Bahadur held no court, made no claim, asked nothing of anyone. He only meditated — like a gardener who sows a seed and waters it for years, without asking when the tree will grow.

The people of Bakala knew him — a quiet, humble man, who spoke little and listened much. Nobody knew that this quiet man would one day become the ninth Guru of the Sikhs.

Twenty-six years — or twenty years?

The count of the years of meditation at Bakala differs between sources — some writings say twenty-six years, some say about twenty years. This book follows twenty-six years in the main story, because that is the count found most often in the traditional accounts — and the other count is recorded here too. The meditation in the bhora is also part of the tradition.

Guru Har Rai and Guru Har Krishan — the years in between

While Tegh Bahadur was living at Bakala, the guruship passed from Har Rai (1644–1661) to Har Krishan (1661–1664). Har Krishan was only five years old when he became Guru — and eight when he died of smallpox in Delhi in 1664.

Pause and think — Twenty-six years of one thing — meditation. Is there something in your life that you do every day, without thinking about when its fruit will come?

4 · Guru Ladho Re — The Search at Bakala · · GURU LADHO RE — THE SEARCH AT BAKALA

The year 1664 came. In Delhi, Guru Har Krishan was ill with smallpox. The sangat asked — after you, who will be the Guru? Har Krishan said only three words — 'Baba Bakale' — the Baba is in Bakala. Then he passed away. He was only eight years old.

The sangat reached Bakala — and what they saw there left them stunned. In Bakala, twenty-two men were sitting outside their houses, each saying — I am the Guru! Each had set up a seat, each had his own followers. The sangat was troubled — who is the true Guru?

Then a trader came — Makhan Shah Lubana. He traded by sea. The tradition tells us that once his ship was caught in a storm — about to sink. Makhan Shah made a vow in his heart — O Guru, if my ship is saved, I will offer the true Guru five hundred gold coins. The ship was saved.

Makhan Shah went to every claimant in Bakala — and before each one he placed only two coins. Every claimant took the two coins and blessed him happily. Nobody asked about the five hundred.

Then he reached a simple house — where a quiet man sat in meditation — Tegh Bahadur. Makhan Shah placed two coins before him too. Tegh Bahadur smiled and said — Makhan Shah, your vow was for five hundred coins — where are the rest?

Makhan Shah — Guru ladho re! I have found the Guru!

Makhan Shah climbed onto a rooftop and shouted — Guru ladho re! Guru ladho re! — I have found the Guru!

The tradition tells us that hearing Makhan Shah's voice, the sangat came running. In August 1664, the sangat formally made Tegh Bahadur the ninth Guru. After twenty-six years of silence, the man who asked for nothing received everything — the guruship, the sangat, and a responsibility that would become the greatest test of his life.

But receiving the guruship was not easy. Dhirmal — the grandson of Hargobind — also claimed the guruship, and behind him stood the power of Delhi. Tegh Bahadur did not quarrel. He went away from Bakala, to a new place near the Shivalik hills — Chak Nanaki — which he named after his mother Nanaki. That same place later became known as Anandpur Sahib.

Twenty-two claimants — the tradition's story

The twenty-two claimants at Bakala and Makhan Shah's vow of five hundred gold coins is the tradition's story — told in the Janamsakhis and Gurbilas literature. The ship, and the test of the two coins, are part of the same tradition. The cry of 'Guru ladho re' is still sung in the sangat today.

Dhirmal — who the claimant was

Dhirmal was the son of Baba Gurditta and the grandson of Guru Hargobind — he was held to be the strongest claimant to the guruship. The tradition says the power of Delhi stood behind him too. This book calls Dhirmal a claimant, not an enemy — because the question of the guruship was settled by service, not by fighting.

Pause and think — Makhan Shah offered two coins to every claimant — and the true Guru remembered the vow of five hundred. Do you think a true Guru is one who asks for more — or one who remembers your vow better than you do?

5 · The Eastern Journey — Anandpur and Dhubri · · THE EASTERN JOURNEY — ANANDPUR AND DHUBRI

After becoming Guru, Tegh Bahadur made Anandpur his seat — near the Shivalik hills, on the banks of the Sutlej river. There he gathered the sangat, ran the langar, and built the Guru's court. But he was not a Guru who stayed in one place — he was a Guru who travelled.

Around 1665, Tegh Bahadur set out on a long journey to the east — as far as Bengal and Assam. On the way he also went to Patna — where his son Gobind Rai was born in 1666.

On the journey he also reached Dhubri — on the banks of the Brahmaputra river, in Assam. The tradition tells us that at Dhubri the Guru sang the bani of the Name to the sangat, and the Guru's name settled in the hearts of the people there. Even today there is a gurdwara of Guru Tegh Bahadur at Dhubri — on the banks of the Brahmaputra, where the sangat comes from far and wide.

On the eastern journey the Guru saw that India was changing. In Delhi ruled the emperor Aurangzeb — and under his rule the pressure on non-Muslims was growing. Orders were coming against temples, and in Kashmir the Pandits were being pressed to change their faith. The Guru returned from the journey — and at Anandpur he prepared the sangat — repeat the Name, share what you eat, and do not fear.

Tegh Bahadur's bani grew deeper in these years. He wrote — the world is fleeting, wealth and youth all pass away — only the Name stays with us. There is no anger in his bani, no fear — only a quiet, deep understanding that this world is a dream, and God alone is true.

Dhubri — the tradition's story

Guru Tegh Bahadur's visit to Dhubri is the tradition's story — his gurdwara still stands at Dhubri on the banks of the Brahmaputra, and the sangat remembers his journey there. The exact years of the journey differ between sources — so this book says 'around 1665' in the main story.

The birth of Gobind Rai — Patna, 1666

The Guru's son Gobind Rai was born in Patna in 1666 — this date is recorded in the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism. Tegh Bahadur was on his eastern journey at the time.

Aurangzeb's pressure — what is certain

Scholars agree that pressure on non-Muslims grew under Aurangzeb's rule — orders against temples came in 1669, and the Pandits of Kashmir were pressed to change their faith. But note — the jizya (the tax on non-Muslims) was reimposed by Aurangzeb in 1679 — four years after the Guru's martyrdom. So this book does not name the jizya as the cause in 1675.

Pause and think — On the eastern journey the Guru joined the sangat far and wide — without the help of any king, without any army. Do you think one person alone can change the world — or does he always need some great power?

6 · The Plea of the Kashmiri Pandits · · THE PLEA OF THE KASHMIRI PANDITS

It was the summer of 1675. One day some people came to Anandpur — from far away Kashmir. Their leader was Pandit Kirpa Ram. They were tired, troubled — and afraid.

The tradition tells us that the Pandits joined their hands before the Guru and said — by the emperor's order, we in Kashmir are being pressed to change our faith. Whoever does not change is killed. We have come to you — because we have heard that you are the one who protects the frightened.

The Guru fell silent. For a long time he said nothing. Then he said slowly — this work asks for the sacrifice of a great soul. Someone is needed who will give his life to protect the faith of others.

The tradition tells us that nearby sat his nine-year-old son Gobind Rai. He said — Father, who is greater than you? You are that great soul.

Gobind Rai — Father, who is greater than you?

Guru Tegh Bahadur — Son, you have spoken true.

The Guru had decided. He would go to Delhi — he would speak to the emperor — and he would protect the Pandits' faith. He knew that this road led to death. But he said — a person who does not stand up for the faith of others cannot stand up for his own faith either.

Before leaving, the Guru made his son Gobind Rai his successor at Anandpur — applying the tilak, handing over the guruship. Then he set out for Delhi with his three companions — Bhai Mati Das, Bhai Sati Das and Bhai Dyal Singh.

The Kashmiri Pandits' plea — the tradition's story

The coming of the Kashmiri Pandits to Anandpur and their plea for help is the tradition's story — told in the Sikh accounts, and there is no contemporary Mughal record of it. Modern scholars (J.S. Grewal, W.H. McLeod) hold different views on what the real cause of the clash between the Guru and Aurangzeb was — some hold it was the defence of faith, some hold there were political causes too. This book tells the tradition's story as the tradition's story, and records the scholars' different view here too.

Gobind Rai's words — the tradition's story

The words of nine-year-old Gobind Rai — 'who is greater than you?' — are also the tradition's story — told in the sangat, and told in this book in that form.

The successor — before leaving

The Guru made his son Gobind Rai his successor before leaving for Delhi — this is recorded in the tradition. Gobind Rai was nine years old at the time.

Pause and think — The Guru knew that going to Delhi meant going towards death — yet he went. Do you think it is right to give your life for the faith of someone else — or should a person protect himself first?

7 · The Journey to Delhi and the Arrest · · THE JOURNEY TO DELHI AND THE ARREST

The Guru set out from Anandpur — on horseback, with his three companions. The road was long — the plains of Punjab, rivers, villages, and everywhere the sangat who stopped them and said — Guru, do not go. But the Guru did not stop.

The tradition tells us that on the way — near Ropar — the emperor's soldiers arrested them. The Guru made no resistance. He went quietly to Delhi — like a person firm in his decision.

In Delhi the Guru was kept in prison. He was brought before the emperor's court — and told — leave your faith. The Guru said — no.

The tradition tells us that the Guru was kept in prison for many weeks — and again and again he was told — change your faith, and your life will be saved. Each time the Guru gave the same answer — no. He kept repeating the Name quietly — as he had repeated it in the bhora at Bakala.

The place of the arrest — the tradition's telling

The place of the Guru's arrest is given in the tradition as near Ropar, at Malikpur. The imprisonment in Delhi and the appearance at court are also in the traditional accounts — there is no contemporary Mughal record of them. This book tells them as the tradition's story.

The weeks in prison — what is certain

The Guru's being kept in prison in Delhi and being asked to change his faith is in the Sikh accounts. The modern historian William Irvine also wrote that the Guru was kept in prison for weeks and asked to change his faith — and that he refused.

Pause and think — The Guru was told — change your faith, and your life will be saved. He said — no. Do you think changing your faith to save your life would be right — or are some things more precious than life?

8 · The Martyrdom — Chandni Chowk · · THE MARTYRDOM — CHANDNI CHOWK

◆ This part is not for younger listeners

Chandni Chowk in Delhi — the biggest market of the emperor's city, where thousands of people came and went. In the winter of 1675, on 24 November 1675, in that very square, Guru Tegh Bahadur was martyred — from afar, in a single moment, without any noise.

The Guru's three companions — Bhai Mati Das, Bhai Sati Das and Bhai Dyal Singh — were martyred in those same days too. All four did not leave their faith — and all four gave their lives.

Before dying, the Guru recited the Japji Sahib — the same bani that Guru Nanak had written. He was calm — as calm as he had been in the bhora at Bakala. He showed no anger, he made no plea. He only kept repeating the Name.

What happened that day in Delhi was not only the death of one man. It was a message — a person who can give his life for the faith of others does not fear any emperor. And that message changed the Sikhs forever.

Today, at that very place in Chandni Chowk, stands Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib — where the Guru was martyred. The sangat goes there, bows its head, and remembers that one man gave his life for the faith of others.

The date of the martyrdom — 24 November or 11 November?

The sources differ on the date of the Guru's martyrdom — by the Nanakshahi calendar of the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee, the Shaheedi Divas is observed every year on 24 November, and most sources give this date. But some sources also give 11 November 1675. This book follows 24 November in the main story, and records the other date here too.

The martyrdom of the three companions — without detail

The martyrdom of Bhai Mati Das, Bhai Sati Das and Bhai Dyal Singh is in the Sikh accounts — and the tradition also records details of how they were killed. This book does not give those details — it only says that they too were martyred in those same days. This book is for young listeners too, so the martyrdom is told in a single line, from afar, without detail.

The recitation of Japji Sahib — the tradition's story

The Guru's reciting the Japji Sahib before his martyrdom is the tradition's story — told in the sangat.

Pause and think — The Guru gave his life for the faith of others — not for his own faith, but for the faith of others. Do you think standing up for someone else's rights is as important as standing up for your own?

9 · The Head to Anandpur — and the Light to Gobind · · THE HEAD TO ANANDPUR — AND THE LIGHT TO GOBIND

After the martyrdom, darkness fell over Delhi. The emperor's soldiers had ordered that no one should touch the Guru's body. But in the dark of night, two disciples came forward — and did what no one else could do.

The tradition tells us that Bhai Jaita took the Guru's head and set out for Anandpur in the dark of night — hundreds of miles, alone, without stopping. He knew that if he were caught, he would be killed. But he kept walking — because the Guru's head had to reach Anandpur.

At Anandpur, nine-year-old Gobind Rai received his father's head and performed its cremation. At that very place today stands Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib, Anandpur.

Meanwhile in Delhi, Lakhi Shah Vanjara took the Guru's body to his house and cremated it — by burning his own house. At that very place today stands Gurdwara Rakab Ganj Sahib — in Delhi, where the sangat still goes.

And so the light of Guru Tegh Bahadur passed into his son. Nine-year-old Gobind Rai now became Guru Gobind Singh — the tenth and last human Guru of the Sikhs. His father had taught him one lesson — fear no one, and frighten no one.

Bhai Jaita and Rakab Ganj — the tradition's story

Bhai Jaita carrying the Guru's head to Anandpur, and Lakhi Shah Vanjara cremating the Guru's body, is the tradition's story — told in the Sikh accounts. Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib at Anandpur and Gurdwara Rakab Ganj Sahib in Delhi still stand at those very places today.

'Hind ki Chadar' — the tradition's honour

'Hind ki Chadar' — the Shield of India, the sheet that protects India — this name was given to Guru Tegh Bahadur by the tradition, after his death. It was not any official title of his time — it was the sangat's honour, which is still joined to his name today. It is the title of this book, and that is written plainly here.

Pause and think — Bhai Jaita walked alone through the night — without any army, without any weapon. Do you think bravery is only in raising a sword — or also in quietly doing the right thing?

To Think About · · TO THINK ABOUT

Tegh Bahadur's story is not the story of a king, nor the story of a warrior. It is the story of a man who meditated quietly for twenty-six years, then was Guru for nine years — and in the end gave his life for the faith of others.

His message fits in a single word — fearlessness. Fear no one — and frighten no one. A person who does not fear, frightens no one either. Tegh Bahadur took no one's faith away, and he did not leave his own faith — he only said that every person has the right to follow his own faith.

Tegh Bahadur's own bani is in the Guru Granth Sahib even today — 116 shabads. Its deepest teaching is this — this world is fleeting, wealth and youth all pass away — only the Name stays with us. There is no anger in his bani, no fear — only a quiet, deep understanding.

After Tegh Bahadur came only one more Guru — Gobind Singh. And in the end that light passed into the Guru Granth Sahib — which is the Guru of the Sikhs even today. His story will come in the next book of this series.

But this ninth book ends here — at Anandpur, with a question — if Tegh Bahadur were here today, what would he say in your home, in your city? Perhaps this — fear no one, frighten no one, and stand up for the rights of others.

Where This Story Comes From · · WHERE THIS STORY COMES FROM

The main source — Tegh Bahadur's own bani

The firmest foundation of this book is Guru Tegh Bahadur's own bani, recorded in the Guru Granth Sahib — 116 shabads, in fifteen ragas. Where this book says 'Tegh Bahadur's own bani', that is its basis.

The count of the shabads — 116 or 115?

The sources differ on the count of Tegh Bahadur's shabads — the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism says 116, and some counts give 115. The difference comes from the way of counting — whether one salok is counted separately or with the shabads. This book writes 116 in the main story, and both counts are recorded here.

The traditional life stories — Janamsakhi and Gurbilas

The stories of Tegh Bahadur's life are found in the Janamsakhis and the Gurbilas literature — above all in Gurbilas Dasvin Patshahi and Mahima Prakash. They were written decades and centuries after Tegh Bahadur's death, and they hold both history and tradition. In this book every story of the tradition is told with 'the tradition tells us', and made plain in its own note.

Modern scholarship

The dates and events of this book have been checked against the work of modern scholars — J.S. Grewal, 'The Sikhs of the Punjab'; W.H. McLeod, 'The Sikhs — History, Religion and Society'; Max Arthur Macauliffe, 'The Sikh Religion'; William Irvine's history of the Mughal period; and the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism (Punjabi University, Patiala). Where scholars and tradition say different things, both are recorded in the book.

One plain thing

In this book Tegh Bahadur is not shown against any faith. He gave his life for the faith of others — and his message was not to divide, but to join. His martyrdom was not the victory of one faith — it was the victory of every person's right to follow his own faith.

The End · · THE END

The story is over — but Tegh Bahadur's fearlessness is not over yet.

In the next book — Guru Gobind Singh, who raised the Khalsa and made the Guru Granth Sahib the Guru.

Waheguru Ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru Ji ki Fateh.
